reading_passages.title: The Real Price of Cheap Clothes [pre-reauthor]
reading_passages.instructions: Read this opinion article, then write a summary as instructed in the question.
reading_passages.body:
A T-shirt can now cost less than a cup of coffee. To a shopper, this looks like good news. To the planet, and to the people who make our clothes, it is a warning sign.

The system behind these low prices is called fast fashion. Brands copy the latest styles, manufacture them at enormous speed, and sell them cheaply, knowing buyers will return within weeks for the next look. To keep prices down, much of this clothing is mass-produced in factories where workers are paid very little. Reports have repeatedly described long hours, unsafe buildings, and wages too low to live on. The cheapness we enjoy in the shop is partly paid for by someone else, somewhere we never see.

The environmental cost is just as serious. Making clothes uses huge amounts of water and energy, and the dyes often pollute rivers. Worse, fast fashion is designed to be temporary. Garments are made to fall out of style — and sometimes to fall apart — within a season, so we keep buying. The result is mountains of waste. A great deal of discarded clothing is burned or buried, and synthetic fabrics can take centuries to break down.

Defenders of fast fashion make two arguments. First, it makes style affordable: a teenager on a small budget can dress well without spending a fortune. Second, the industry provides jobs in countries that need them. Both points are true, and they should not be dismissed. Cheap clothing is not simply evil, and the workers who depend on these jobs would suffer if every factory closed overnight.

But affordability and jobs do not require a system built on waste and low pay. The problem is not that clothes are cheap; it is that the true costs are hidden and pushed onto others. There are better paths. Buying fewer, better-made items reduces waste. Choosing second-hand keeps clothing in use for longer. Supporting brands that pay fairly and produce less rewards the right behaviour. None of these alone will fix the industry, but together they shift the pressure.

In the end, the question is not whether we can afford fast fashion. Clearly we can — the prices are tiny. The real question is whether we can afford its true cost: the rivers, the waste, and the people behind the seams. Once you have seen that price, the cheap T-shirt never looks quite so cheap again.

reading_passages.title: What My Clothes Say About Me
reading_passages.instructions: Read the four accounts and answer the questions.
reading_passages.body:
We asked four young people what their clothes mean to them.

A — PRIYA
For me, clothes are about comfort, nothing more. I wear the same few outfits on rotation, and I genuinely don't notice what anyone else has on. People sometimes assume I'm not interested in how I look — but it's not that. I just decided years ago that I didn't want to spend energy thinking about it. Getting dressed in ten seconds is a kind of freedom.

B — MARCUS
I save for months to buy one good piece. I'd rather own three jackets that last ten years than thirty that fall apart. My friends think I'm extravagant, but it's the opposite — when you count the cost per wear, the expensive coat is the cheap one. What I can't stand is throwing clothes away. A well-made thing should outlive the trend that made it popular.

C — LENA
My style changes constantly, and that's the whole point. One month I dress like the 1970s, the next like a film I just watched. Clothes are how I try on different versions of myself before I decide who I want to be. Some people find one look and keep it forever; I'd find that suffocating. For me, getting dressed is play.

D — SAM
I dress to fit in, and I'm not ashamed of it. At my age, standing out is risky — I've seen what happens to people who get it wrong. So I watch what the group wears and I match it. It's not that I have no taste; it's that belonging matters more to me than being noticed. My clothes are a way of saying: I'm one of you.

reading_passages.title: The Trainers Everyone Wanted (Backup)
reading_passages.instructions: Backup passage (alternate, same skill: language & effect). Read the personal essay and answer the questions.
reading_passages.body:
The trainers arrived at our school like weather. One week, no one had them. The next, they were on every other pair of feet, white and gleaming, as if a single cloud had rained shoes overnight.

I did not have them. I told myself I did not care, and for a few days the lie held. Then I began to notice the small things: the quick glance down at my old shoes, the way a conversation paused, just slightly, when someone new arrived in the famous white. The trainers were not just trainers. They were a password, and I did not know it.

What surprised me was how fast want became need. I had been perfectly happy with my scuffed black shoes on Monday. By Friday they felt like a confession — proof that I was outside, behind, not quite one of the group. Nothing about the shoes had changed. Only the air around them had.

My mother asked why these particular trainers mattered so much. I could not explain it, because the real answer sounded foolish out loud: they mattered because everyone else had decided they mattered. That is the strange power of a crowd. It can take an ordinary object and fill it with meaning, the way a single lit window can make a whole dark street look warm.

In the end I did not buy them. The hunger faded, as these hungers do, and by the next term the white trainers were old news, replaced by something else. But I have never forgotten the lesson hidden in those few weeks: how easily a crowd can tell you what to want — and how quietly it takes the wanting back.

reading_passages.title: Slow Fashion: Buying Less, Choosing Better (Backup)
reading_passages.instructions: Backup passage (alternate, same skill: summary writing). Read the article, then write a summary as instructed.
reading_passages.body:
If fast fashion is the problem, what is the answer? A growing movement says it is not to buy nothing, but to buy differently. Its name is slow fashion, and the idea is simple: fewer clothes, chosen with more care, and kept for longer.

Slow fashion starts with a question most shoppers never ask: how long will I actually wear this? A cheap top bought on impulse may be worn twice before it is forgotten. A well-made jacket, chosen carefully, might last ten years. Spread across all those years, the expensive jacket can work out cheaper — and it creates far less waste. Buying less, supporters argue, is not about having less. It is about owning things you genuinely use.

The movement also values quality and repair. For decades, we have been taught to throw clothes away the moment they tear. Slow fashion brings back older habits: sewing on a button, patching a knee, taking a jacket to be mended rather than replaced. Some schools and community groups now run repair workshops, where students learn skills their grandparents took for granted.

A third idea is keeping clothes in circulation. Swapping with friends, donating to charity shops, and buying second-hand all keep garments out of landfill and in use. One person's unwanted coat becomes another person's favourite find. A jacket that has grown dull in one wardrobe can feel almost new in another, and nothing fresh has to be manufactured for the swap to happen.

Critics raise a fair objection. Well-made, ethically produced clothing is often more expensive, and not everyone can pay more at the checkout, even if it saves money later. Slow fashion, they warn, can become a luxury for the well-off, while ordinary shoppers are blamed for buying cheap. This is a real risk, and any honest version of the movement must take it seriously.

Yet slow fashion need not be expensive. Its cheapest forms — wearing what you own for longer, repairing instead of replacing, buying second-hand — cost little or nothing. The shift it asks for is less about money than about mindset: treating clothes as things to value rather than things to use up.

The fashion industry will not change because of one shopper. But every garment kept for an extra year, every repair, every swapped jacket is a small vote for a different system. Slow fashion is not about owning a perfect wardrobe. It is about asking better questions before we buy.

reading_passages.title: The Comeback of Old Clothes (Backup)
reading_passages.instructions: Backup passage (alternate, same skill: skimming & scanning). Read the feature and answer the questions.
reading_passages.body:
My grandmother kept everything. When she passed her old wardrobe to me, I expected to throw most of it away. Instead, my friends asked where I had bought my new jacket. It was forty years old.

Something has changed in the way young people shop. For a long time, the newest clothes were the most wanted. Now, more and more teenagers are proud to wear second-hand pieces. Thrift shops that once felt forgotten are full again on weekends, and online resale apps have millions of users. A look that signals you bought something used — a worn denim jacket, a faded band T-shirt — has become, oddly, fashionable.

Part of the reason is cost. Used clothes are cheaper, and a student budget only stretches so far. But that is not the whole story. Wearing something old also feels different from wearing something everyone can buy in the same shop. It is harder to copy. When a friend admires a jacket that no longer exists in any store, the compliment feels personal.

There is an environmental reason too. Many young shoppers now know that cheap, fast-made clothing creates enormous waste. Choosing second-hand is one small way to push back. Each reused garment is one less that has to be made, dyed, and shipped, and one less that ends up buried or burned. It is a small choice on its own, but small choices, repeated by enough people, slowly begin to add up. For them, an old coat is not a step down; it is a quiet statement.

Of course, vintage has itself become a trend, with all the speed that brings. Some shops now make brand-new clothes designed to look old and worn. The cycle never really stops — it only changes shape. Still, the next time someone asks where you got your jacket, there may be real pleasure in answering: it was my grandmother's.

reading_passages.title: The Grey Army
reading_passages.instructions: Read this personal essay and answer the questions, paying attention to the writer's use of language and its effect.
reading_passages.body:
Every morning, two thousand of us pour through the gates in the same grey. From the bridge above, we are not students; we are a tide, a single grey animal breathing in and out at the bell. Our uniform is meant to make us equal. Sometimes it just makes us disappear.

I have worn this grey for five years, and I have felt both things it does. On my worst mornings, when my shoes are scuffed and my hair will not sit, the uniform is a kindness — a curtain I can hide behind, where no one measures me against anyone else. We are all the same grey, and the same grey cannot be mocked.

But there are other mornings. Mornings when I want to be a colour, not a crowd. When the grey feels less like a curtain and more like a lid, pressing two thousand restless lives into one flat shape. On those mornings I notice the rebellions, tiny and everywhere: a bright lace, a folded sleeve, a badge worn just out of a teacher's sightline. Small flames, flickering against the grey.

That is the truth no rule can erase. You can dress us the same, but you cannot make us the same. The need to be ourselves does not vanish; it only shrinks, hides, waits. Press it down here, and it pops up there — in a drawing inside a shoe, a song hummed in a corridor, a way of walking that is unmistakably yours.

So dress us in grey, if you must. We will wear it. But look closely at the tide as it passes, and you will see it everywhere: the colour leaking through. We were never one grey animal. We were two thousand, each of us burning quietly to be seen.

reading_passages.title: The Uniform I Drew On (Backup)
reading_passages.instructions: Backup passage (alternate, same skill: inference & viewpoint). Read the personal essay and answer the questions.
reading_passages.body:
At my school, everyone wore the same grey uniform. The rule was strict: no jewellery, no unusual shoes, nothing to mark you out. The idea, our teachers said, was fairness — if we all looked the same, no one could be judged for what they could or could not afford. I understood the reason. I still hated it.

It was not that I wanted expensive things. It was that the grey felt like a lid pressed over the whole school, flattening everyone into the same shape. We were two thousand students, and from the top of the stairs we looked like one grey crowd.

So I found small ways to stay myself. Inside my left shoe, where no teacher would ever look, I drew a tiny pattern in blue pen and redrew it every week. I knew it was there. On the bus home, the moment we crossed the school gate, I would push my sleeves up in a particular way, fold my collar a certain way — tiny changes that meant nothing to anyone else and everything to me.

I used to think this made me strange. Later I learned that almost everyone did something similar. My friend kept a bright lining sewn into her plain bag. Another boy wore odd socks on purpose, one rule he could break without being caught. To a stranger, these gestures would have meant nothing at all. That was exactly the point: they were ours, private and unofficial, a small language the uniform could see but never quite read. None of us were rebels. We were simply looking for a crack of light, a way to say I am still here under the grey.

I do not think uniforms are wrong. There is something restful about not competing over clothes every morning, and I have read that students argue less about appearance when everyone dresses the same. But I have also come to believe that the need to express who you are does not switch off because a rule tells it to. It just goes quiet, and finds smaller places to live — a drawing in a shoe, a folded sleeve, a hidden colour.

When I left that school, I kept the shoes. The pattern in blue pen is faded now, almost gone. But I remember exactly why I drew it: not to be seen by anyone else, but to remind myself, on the greyest mornings, that I had not disappeared.

reading_passages.title: How a Trend Travels
reading_passages.instructions: Read this magazine feature about fashion trends and answer the questions that follow.
reading_passages.body:
Five years ago, almost no one at my school wore wide-legged jeans. Now, on any morning, half the corridor is in them. I started to wonder how a single look spreads so fast — and why it fades just as quickly.

A trend usually begins small. A designer shows something unusual on a runway, or a teenager in one city films a thirty-second clip of an outfit. Most of these ideas go nowhere. But every so often one of them is picked up by an influencer with millions of followers, and within days it is everywhere. Last spring, a student in Seoul posted a video of herself styling an oversized blazer with shorts. The clip went viral. Three weeks later, shops in Bangkok were selling almost the same blazer, and my classmates were wearing it without knowing where it came from.

This is the strange thing about modern fashion: a look can travel from one bedroom to a hundred countries before anyone can explain why it matters. Social media has made the journey faster than ever. In the past, a style might take a year to move from a fashion capital to an ordinary high street. Today it can happen in a fortnight.

Speed has a cost, though. The faster a trend rises, the faster it falls. By the time a look becomes truly mainstream — sold cheaply in every shop, worn by everyone — the people who started it have usually moved on. What felt fresh in March can feel tired by September. Some styles return years later as a revival, dressed up as something new, and the cycle begins again.

So the next time you notice everyone suddenly wearing the same thing, it is worth asking two questions. Where did this come from? And how long before it disappears? The answers say a lot — not only about clothes, but about how quickly we copy one another.

reading_passages.title: Why I Stopped Dressing for Other People
reading_passages.instructions: Read this personal essay, then answer the questions and complete the notes as instructed.
reading_passages.body:
For most of secondary school, I dressed to disappear. I chose whatever the others were wearing — the same shoes, the same bag, the same neutral colours — because being noticed felt dangerous. If no one looked at me, no one could judge me. It worked, in a way. I blended in completely. I also felt completely invisible.

The change began with a coat. I found it in a second-hand shop: deep green, slightly too big, with large gold buttons. It was nothing like what anyone at school wore. For two weeks it hung in my wardrobe while I argued with myself. Wearing it would mean standing out, and standing out meant questions.

I wore it on a Monday. The first comment came before I reached my classroom — but it was not the comment I feared. I love that, a girl I barely knew said. It is so you. I had no idea what so me meant; I had spent years making sure I had no recognisable style at all. Yet the phrase stayed with me. For the first time, my clothes had said something, and someone had listened.

After that, I began to experiment. Not dramatically — I am not a bold dresser even now. But I started choosing things because I liked them, not because they were safe. A scarf in a colour that made me happy. Shoes that were comfortable rather than fashionable. Slowly, my wardrobe began to feel less like a uniform and more like a reflection of me.

What surprised me most was the effect on my confidence. I had always assumed confidence came first, and that confident people then dressed boldly. For me it was the other way around. Choosing clothes that felt true made me stand a little straighter. The green coat did not make me a different person. It simply let the person I already was become visible.

I am not saying everyone should dress to be noticed. Some people feel most themselves in plain, quiet clothes, and that is its own kind of honesty. The point is not loud or quiet, bold or modest. The point is choice — wearing what reflects you, rather than what hides you. Looking back, the saddest part of those early years was not that I dressed badly. It was that I dressed like someone trying very hard not to exist.

These days, when a younger student asks me for advice about clothes, I give the same short answer every time: wear the coat.

listening_tracks.title: How I Dress, and Why: Six Speakers
listening_tracks.instructions: You will hear six people (Speakers 1-6) say why they dress the way they do. Match each speaker to the statement (A-H). There are TWO extra statements you will not need. A: I dress to feel confident on hard days. B: I copy whatever my friends wear. C: I dress to express my culture and where I am from. D: I prefer plain clothes so people focus on what I say. E: I buy only second-hand to reduce waste. F: I change my style completely depending on my mood. G: I dress to be comfortable above all else. H: I follow whatever is trending online. [Audio to be produced.]
listening_tracks.script_text:
Speaker 1: Mornings when I feel low, I put on my brightest jacket. It is like armour. Once it is on, I can face the day.

Speaker 2: I will not buy anything new any more. Everything I wear has had a life before me — it keeps clothes out of the bin.

Speaker 3: Honestly? I wear whatever is blowing up online that week. If a look is everywhere on my feed, it ends up on me.

Speaker 4: I keep my clothes simple and plain. In a meeting, I want people listening to my ideas, not staring at my outfit.

Speaker 5: My grandmother's patterns, the colours from home — I wear them on purpose. My clothes say where I come from.

Speaker 6: Comfort wins, every time. If I cannot move, run for the bus, sit on the floor — I will not wear it, however nice it looks.

listening_tracks.script_text:
Thanks for having me. A year ago I tried something I called the thirty-item challenge. The idea was simple: for one whole year, I would wear only thirty pieces of clothing. Everything else went into a box in the garage.

Why did I do it? Honestly, not to save the planet — at least not at first. My wardrobe was so full I could never find anything, and I was tired of buying things I wore once. I wanted to see what would happen if I stopped.

There were rules. Underwear and sports kit did not count, but everything else did — shoes, coats, the lot. If I wanted something new, I had to give something away first. One in, one out.

The first month was the hardest. I kept reaching for things that were now in the garage. But by the second month, getting dressed had become faster, not slower. With fewer choices, I actually wore my favourite things more often.

The biggest surprise was that no one noticed. I had been sure people judged my clothes every day. In a whole year, exactly one person commented — and it was to say I always looked put together. The audience I was dressing for, it turned out, was mostly in my own head.

Did I save money? Yes, a lot. But the real change was how I shopped afterwards. Now, before I buy anything, I ask one question: will this earn its place? If I cannot imagine wearing it thirty times, I leave it on the rail.

I am not telling you to count your clothes. The number is not the point. The point is to own things you actually use — and to notice how little the crowd is really watching.

listening_tracks.script_text:
HOST: Niran, you started a clothes-swap at your school. How did it begin?
NIRAN: Almost by accident. I had a bag of clothes I had grown out of, a friend had the same, and we just traded. Within a term, two hundred students were doing it.
HOST: Were you trying to make a statement about fast fashion?
NIRAN: Not at first. I will not pretend I started it to save the world — I started it because buying new all the time was draining my money. The environmental part came later, once I saw how much we were throwing away.
HOST: Some people say swaps are just a trend that will fade.
NIRAN: Maybe the word swap will fade. But I do not think the habit will. Once you have worn something brilliant that cost you nothing, paying full price for a copy everyone owns feels a bit silly.
HOST: Do you ever miss buying new things?
NIRAN: Honestly, sometimes. There is a thrill in something new that a swap cannot quite match. I am not going to lie about that. But the thrill fades in a week, and the regret lasts longer.
HOST: What would you say to someone who thinks their choices are too small to matter?
NIRAN: I used to think that too. One person swapping a jacket changes nothing. But two hundred people, every term — that is hundreds of clothes that were not bought new and were not binned. Small only stays small if you stay alone.
HOST: Finally, has it changed how you see your own style?
NIRAN: Completely. I used to dress to keep up. Now I dress to use what I have well. It is quieter, but it feels more like me.

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: How a Trend Travels
listening_tracks.script_text:
Five years ago, almost no one at my school wore wide-legged jeans. Now, on any morning, half the corridor is in them. I started to wonder how a single look spreads so fast — and why it fades just as quickly.

A trend usually begins small. A designer shows something unusual on a runway, or a teenager in one city films a thirty-second clip of an outfit. Most of these ideas go nowhere. But every so often one of them is picked up by an influencer with millions of followers, and within days it is everywhere. Last spring, a student in Seoul posted a video of herself styling an oversized blazer with shorts. The clip went viral. Three weeks later, shops in Bangkok were selling almost the same blazer, and my classmates were wearing it without knowing where it came from.

This is the strange thing about modern fashion: a look can travel from one bedroom to a hundred countries before anyone can explain why it matters. Social media has made the journey faster than ever. In the past, a style might take a year to move from a fashion capital to an ordinary high street. Today it can happen in a fortnight.

Speed has a cost, though. The faster a trend rises, the faster it falls. By the time a look becomes truly mainstream — sold cheaply in every shop, worn by everyone — the people who started it have usually moved on. What felt fresh in March can feel tired by September. Some styles return years later as a revival, dressed up as something new, and the cycle begins again.

So the next time you notice everyone suddenly wearing the same thing, it is worth asking two questions. Where did this come from? And how long before it disappears? The answers say a lot — not only about clothes, but about how quickly we copy one another.

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: The Grey Army
listening_tracks.script_text:
Every morning, two thousand of us pour through the gates in the same grey. From the bridge above, we are not students; we are a tide, a single grey animal breathing in and out at the bell. Our uniform is meant to make us equal. Sometimes it just makes us disappear.

I have worn this grey for five years, and I have felt both things it does. On my worst mornings, when my shoes are scuffed and my hair will not sit, the uniform is a kindness — a curtain I can hide behind, where no one measures me against anyone else. We are all the same grey, and the same grey cannot be mocked.

But there are other mornings. Mornings when I want to be a colour, not a crowd. When the grey feels less like a curtain and more like a lid, pressing two thousand restless lives into one flat shape. On those mornings I notice the rebellions, tiny and everywhere: a bright lace, a folded sleeve, a badge worn just out of a teacher's sightline. Small flames, flickering against the grey.

That is the truth no rule can erase. You can dress us the same, but you cannot make us the same. The need to be ourselves does not vanish; it only shrinks, hides, waits. Press it down here, and it pops up there — in a drawing inside a shoe, a song hummed in a corridor, a way of walking that is unmistakably yours.

So dress us in grey, if you must. We will wear it. But look closely at the tide as it passes, and you will see it everywhere: the colour leaking through. We were never one grey animal. We were two thousand, each of us burning quietly to be seen.

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: The Real Price of Cheap Clothes
listening_tracks.script_text:
A T-shirt can now cost less than a cup of coffee. To a shopper, this looks like good news. To the planet, and to the people who make our clothes, it is a warning sign.

The system behind these low prices is called fast fashion. Brands copy the latest styles, manufacture them at enormous speed, and sell them cheaply, knowing buyers will return within weeks for the next look. To keep prices down, much of this clothing is mass-produced in factories where workers are paid very little. Reports have repeatedly described long hours, unsafe buildings, and wages too low to live on. The cheapness we enjoy in the shop is partly paid for by someone else, somewhere we never see.

The environmental cost is just as serious. Making clothes uses huge amounts of water and energy, and the dyes often pollute rivers. Worse, fast fashion is designed to be temporary. Garments are made to fall out of style — and sometimes to fall apart — within a season, so we keep buying. The result is mountains of waste. A great deal of discarded clothing is burned or buried, and synthetic fabrics can take centuries to break down.

Defenders of fast fashion make two arguments. First, it makes style affordable: a teenager on a small budget can dress well without spending a fortune. Second, the industry provides jobs in countries that need them. Both points are true, and they should not be dismissed. Cheap clothing is not simply evil, and the workers who depend on these jobs would suffer if every factory closed overnight.

But affordability and jobs do not require a system built on waste and low pay. The problem is not that clothes are cheap; it is that the true costs are hidden and pushed onto others. There are better paths. Buying fewer, better-made items reduces waste. Choosing second-hand keeps clothing in use for longer. Supporting brands that pay fairly and produce less rewards the right behaviour. None of these alone will fix the industry, but together they shift the pressure.

In the end, the question is not whether we can afford fast fashion. Clearly we can — the prices are tiny. The real question is whether we can afford its true cost: the rivers, the waste, and the people behind the seams. Once you have seen that price, the cheap T-shirt never looks quite so cheap again.

listening_tracks.title: Read-Aloud: Why I Stopped Dressing for Other People
listening_tracks.script_text:
For most of secondary school, I dressed to disappear. I chose whatever the others were wearing — the same shoes, the same bag, the same neutral colours — because being noticed felt dangerous. If no one looked at me, no one could judge me. It worked, in a way. I blended in completely. I also felt completely invisible.

The change began with a coat. I found it in a second-hand shop: deep green, slightly too big, with large gold buttons. It was nothing like what anyone at school wore. For two weeks it hung in my wardrobe while I argued with myself. Wearing it would mean standing out, and standing out meant questions.

I wore it on a Monday. The first comment came before I reached my classroom — but it was not the comment I feared. I love that, a girl I barely knew said. It is so you. I had no idea what so me meant; I had spent years making sure I had no recognisable style at all. Yet the phrase stayed with me. For the first time, my clothes had said something, and someone had listened.

After that, I began to experiment. Not dramatically — I am not a bold dresser even now. But I started choosing things because I liked them, not because they were safe. A scarf in a colour that made me happy. Shoes that were comfortable rather than fashionable. Slowly, my wardrobe began to feel less like a uniform and more like a reflection of me.

What surprised me most was the effect on my confidence. I had always assumed confidence came first, and that confident people then dressed boldly. For me it was the other way around. Choosing clothes that felt true made me stand a little straighter. The green coat did not make me a different person. It simply let the person I already was become visible.

I am not saying everyone should dress to be noticed. Some people feel most themselves in plain, quiet clothes, and that is its own kind of honesty. The point is not loud or quiet, bold or modest. The point is choice — wearing what reflects you, rather than what hides you. Looking back, the saddest part of those early years was not that I dressed badly. It was that I dressed like someone trying very hard not to exist.

These days, when a younger student asks me for advice about clothes, I give the same short answer every time: wear the coat.

writing_tasks.model_answer:
My aunt Lena has the most distinctive style of anyone I know. The moment she walks into a room, heads turn — not because she is loud, but because everything about her appearance feels deliberate.

She is wearing, as always, a long charcoal-grey coat with a single bright scarf, a deep glowing red that catches the eye. Her silver rings, worn on almost every finger, are bold yet somehow understated. Her short grey hair is neatly cut, and she is carrying an old leather bag that she has owned for years. Nothing is new; everything has been chosen with care.

That red scarf is her signature. To me, her style is a quiet form of self-expression — confident, calm and completely her own. It says that you do not need to follow every trend to have a strong identity. Long after she leaves, it is that single flash of red, against all the grey, that stays in my mind.

Most days, you'll find me in the same simple uniform of my own choosing: dark jeans, a plain T-shirt, and whatever jacket suits the weather. Nothing flashy.

If I had to describe my style, I'd call it quiet and practical. I like clothes that do their job and don't shout for attention. Comfort comes first, but I do care that things match.

It has changed, though. A couple of years ago, I tried hard to wear exactly what everyone else wore. I spent money on trainers I didn't even like, just to fit in. Slowly I realised I was more comfortable, in every sense, dressing simply.

I'll be honest: I buy new clothes more often than I should, usually without thinking where they came from.

But I've started to learn a little about fast fashion — how clothes made very cheaply and very fast often come at a hidden cost, both to the planet and to the people who sew them.

Now, I want to grant the other side fairly. Cheap clothing isn't simply the villain. For many families it is the only affordable option, and for many workers these jobs are a real and valued source of income. We shouldn't pretend otherwise.

So yes, the way we shop should change — slowly, and without pretending the people who make our clothes don't depend on the work.

speaking_tasks.model_response:
Good afternoon. Our side stands against banning fast fashion — not because we deny its harm, but because a ban is the wrong tool.

Our first reason is people. Millions earn their living making these clothes; remove the industry overnight and you remove their wages, with nothing ready to replace them. Our second reason is fairness at home: for a family on a tight budget, cheap clothing is sometimes the only way to dress growing children. A ban punishes them first.

Now, the other side will say that only a ban is strong enough to force change. We understand the frustration — gentle requests have achieved little. But look closer: a ban hides the problem rather than fixing it. Make the rules instead — safe factories, fair pay, less waste.

So we close where we began: don't ban the industry that clothes and feeds millions. Reform it, and reform it properly. That is how real change lasts.

Thank you.

Honestly, I prefer to fit in — most of the time, anyway. There's a kind of comfort in not being looked at.

I remember a day I wore something bold to a party, sure it looked great, and walked in to find everyone else in plain black. I felt different in the worst way, and I wanted to disappear.
